claims.claim: PSEG combines regulated grid infrastructure with 3,758 MW of carbon-free baseload nuclear capacity, linking electricity reliability and rising peak demand to transmission/distribution investment and firm generation.

Nuclear baseload can strengthen resilience under rising electricity demand, while successor bottlenecks include transmission capacity, regulatory recovery, financing and fuel/outage execution rather than generation capacity alone.

risks.risk: Large capital needs shift the bottleneck toward financing, regulatory recovery and execution quality.

unknowns.unknown: Timing and economics of prospective multi-year nuclear output contracts remain unresolved.

falsifiers: Persistent reliability deterioration despite capital deployment would weaken the infrastructure-resilience thesis.
Nuclear availability or contracting economics materially below assumptions would weaken firm-generation advantage.

claims.claim: The $24B-$28B capital program can improve system capability, but higher depreciation and interest expense demonstrate that investment scale itself is not proof of value creation.

Current earnings and restoration performance support execution credibility, while future rate-case recovery, financing mix and nuclear contract economics remain material uncertainty rather than present contradictions.

risks.risk: Financing costs and depreciation can dilute benefits from incremental rate-base growth.
Regulatory recovery and customer affordability can constrain realized returns.
Nuclear operational or contracting setbacks can reduce the value of firm-generation exposure.

unknowns.unknown: Current evidence does not establish final financing mix, future rate-case outcomes or nuclear contract pricing.
